B2 First for Schools Reading and Use of English Part 3

Aims of the lesson   to familiarise students with what is required in Part 3 of the Reading and Use of
                          English Paper: Word-building or Word Formation
Time needed
Materials required   to give student strategies for completing Part 3

                    50 minutes

                     Student’s worksheet (one copy for each student)
                     Sample task (one per student)
                     Answer sheet (copy for each student from the relevant pages of the Reading

                         and Use of English section of the B2 First for Schools Handbook)

Procedure

1. Write the word ‘know’ on the board and write the table as below only leave it empty. Ask the
     students to put the word know into the table and put it in the verb column. Brainstorm another word
     which can be formed from ‘know’ and put this in the table as well. In pairs or small groups, give them
     two minutes to brainstorm all the other words formed from ‘know’ for this. When you see they have
     finished, write the words they have come up with on the board, putting them into the table:

verb                   noun    adje ctive               adv erb
                    knowledge  (can you add a prefix    (can you add a prefix or a
know                           or a suffix?)            suffix?)
knew                           knowing                  knowingly
known
knowing                        unknowing                unknowingly
                               known                    knowledgeably

                               unknown
                               knowledgeable
                               knowable
                               unknowable

2. Explain that you are going to look at Part 3 of the Reading and Use of English paper, in which their
    ability to build words is tested.

3. Write the title ‘Skyscraper? No, ‘water-scraper!’ on the board and ask the class what they
    think the text will be about.

4. Give out the Sample task and ask the students to read the text quickly to see if any of their
    predictions were correct. They should ignore the gaps in the text for now. Allow about 3
    minutes for this, then elicit what the text is about and if they were correct (it’s about a very tall
    building built on the seabed – it doesn’t exist, but it’s a possible idea for buildings of the
    future).

5. Elicit what candidates have to do to complete this task. Focus on the words in capitals at the
    end of some of the lines (tell the students that these are called stem words), and using the
    example, establish that they need to form a new word using these stem words to complete the
    gaps. Look at the example (competition), ask them what part of speech it is (look at the table
    for ‘know’ you have just done to give them alternatives if they aren’t sure), and elicit that this is
    a noun. Go through the text with the whole class, eliciting which part of speech each gap
    could be filled with (see Sample Task Answer key, table second column). Deciding what word
    class is needed in each of the gaps is also a very important strategy, which students should
    practise regularly.

6. Divide the students into two groups. Ask each group to line up in alphabetical order, using
    first names only.

7. Give the board pen to the first person in the class alphabetically (if both groups are headed by
    someone with the same name, toss a coin!)

8. The first person comes to the board and writes the word they (and their group, who can help)
    think is correct for the first gap. If it’s correct, the next person in the same group can come to
    the board and write the next word. If they make a mistake, the board pen passes to the other
    group. Mark the words so each group can keep a tally of their correct answers. The winning
    group is the one with the most correct words.

9. Look at the correct answers on the board with the class. Elicit how the stem word has been
    changed (see Answer key). Tell the students that some answers are possible by reading just
    a word or two before or after the gap. For example, ‘competition’: it is clear that a noun in
    required from the word ‘a’ earlier in the sentence. However, there are other answers where
    the whole paragraph is needed. This is especially true where negative prefixes are required,
    as in the example ‘impossible’ here. Reading the whole text through before trying to complete
    any of the gaps is a very useful strategy for this task. Candidates should always bear in mind
    the meaning of the text as a whole as well as the language on either side of each gap.

10. Give out the Student’s worksheet and ask students to work in pairs/ small groups to decide if the
    sentences about B2 First for Schools Reading and Use of English Part 3 are true or false. If they
    think a sentence is false, they should try to correct it.

11. Feed back with the whole class, eliciting corrections to the false sentences and encouraging
    students to write down the corrections (see Key).

12. Give students an Answer sheet each so they can see where they will record their answers.

13. Finally ask the students to look at the example text and to tell you which part of speech hasn’t

been addressed. The answer is adverbs. Tell them that this is a very common question as in the

sentence: ‘He didn’t care about his appearance and dressed  . Give the class stem

word TIDY. This is a good example of a more difficult question as it requires changes at both ends.

Elicit the answer ‘untidily’. Tell the students to look in their coursebooks and find an example of an

adverb in a word building.

Suggested follow-up activity
• Give students words and ask them to think of words they can form from them. If dictionaries

     are available, these could be used to check answers, but remind students that they won’t be
     able to use dictionaries in the exam. E.g.
 belief (believe, disbelieve, believable, unbelievable, believing, disbelieving, unbelieving,
     believer, unbeliever...)
 beauty (beautiful, beautify, beautification, beauties...)
 deep (depth, deepen, deeper, deepest...)
     Feedback in this case can be as a game of tennis. If the class is in two groups, the team
     serves with their first word, for example ‘believe’, the second group returns with for example
     ‘believable’, the first groups gives another word, for example ‘disbelief’. The winner of the point
     is the team with the most answers, so the rally continues until one team has no more words.
     The serve for the next stem word goes to the next team. To gather stem words simply look
     through some past paper part 3’s, you will soon see that there are words which very regularly
     come up.
• Practise recognising words in texts, songs, etc which are formed from a stem word, and also
     recognising what word class these words are.
• Ask students to find words from which lots of other words can be formed – they could bring
     them in to challenge their classmates in a future class.

Student’s worksheet

 Decide whether the following sentences about Part 3 of the Reading and Use of English paper are
 TRUE or FALSE. Correct the sentences which are wrong.
 1. There are ten gaps to fill.
 2. You can only write one word in each gap.
 3. The gaps are on different lines from the stem words.
 4. Part 3 covers mostly grammar but vocabulary is also involved.
 5. Sometimes you have to read beyond the sentence to get the answer.
 6. There are 2 marks for each correct answer.
 7. Minor spelling mistakes are permitted.
 8. Answers must be written on a separate answer sheet in capital letters.
 9. Words can be negatives or plurals of the given stem word.
 10. Some stem words remain the same.

Sample task

For questions 17 – 24, read the text below. Use the word given in capitals at the end of some of
the lines to form a word that fits in the gap in the same line. There is an example at the beginning
(0).

Write your answers IN CAPITAL LETTERS on the separate answer sheet.
